```{r}
#| label: setup
# The report only reads what run_all.R saved; it never refits anything.
library(ggplot2)
source("R/functions.R")
cfg <- read_config("config.yml")
out <- \(f) readRDS(file.path(cfg$paths$output, f))

table <- nanoparquet::read_parquet(cfg$paths$table)
calls <- out("calls.rds")
bins  <- out("bins.rds")
cmp   <- out("comparison.rds")

theme_set(theme_minimal())
pal  <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(8, "Dark2")
grey <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(9, "Greys")
model_cols <- setNames(pal[1:4], model_labels)
lab <- \(m) factor(model_labels[m], levels = model_labels)
n <- \(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

# Data

The data are one week of North Atlantic right whale up-calls logged by an
analyst on one channel of the NOPP6 recorder in Stellwagen Bank National
Marine Sanctuary (DCLDE 2013). Every step from the raw log to the counts
the models see is shown here, with the number of rows it leaves.

## From raw log to bins

```{r}
#| label: steps
steps <- tibble::tibble(
  Step = c("Raw log, built into the dictionary's table",
           paste("Keep confidence:", toString(cfg$prepare$confidence_keep)),
           "Collapse rows sharing a start time",
           paste0(cfg$bin_width, "-minute bins (EST)")),
  Rows = c(nrow(table),
           sum(table$confidence %in% cfg$prepare$confidence_keep),
           nrow(calls), nrow(bins))
)
knitr::kable(dplyr::mutate(steps, Rows = n(Rows)), align = "lr")
```

1. **Build** (`R/01_build.R`). The raw log becomes the table described in
   `data/data-dict.yaml`. All `r n(nrow(table))` rows are kept, in log order,
   and the table is checked against the dictionary with `datadict`. The run
   stops if they disagree.
2. **Prepare** (`R/02_prepare.R`). Only calls the analyst marked as
   `r toString(cfg$prepare$confidence_keep)` are kept; this is
   `confidence_keep` in `config.yml`. Rows sharing a start time are
   collapsed to one, then the calls are sorted by time.
3. **Bin** (`R/03_bin.R`). Calls are counted in `r cfg$bin_width`-minute
   bins on local standard time (EST) over the whole window. Empty bins are
   zero counts, not missing: recording was continuous. The bins hold all
   `r n(sum(bins$y))` prepared calls.

## Traps in the log

**The log is not in time order.** It was written as one file per local
day, and within a day some passages were logged out of sequence. In log
order the start time steps backwards
**`r sum(diff(table$time) < 0)` times**, by up to
`r round(max(-diff(table$time)[diff(table$time) < 0]) / 3600, 1)` hours.
Anything temporal (gaps, rates, lags) is computed after sorting by time.

```{r}
#| label: backward
#| fig-height: 3
steps_back <- tibble::tibble(row = seq_len(nrow(table) - 1),
                             step = as.numeric(diff(table$time), units = "hours")) |>
  dplyr::filter(step < 0)
ggplot(steps_back, aes(row, -step)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[2]) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Row of the log", y = "Backward step (hours, log scale)",
       title = "Every place the log's start time goes backwards")
```

**Five pairs of rows share a start time.** They are probably the same call
logged twice. With `dedupe_same_start: true` each pair keeps its
higher-confidence row.

```{r}
#| label: duplicates
table |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::n() > 1, .by = time) |>
  dplyr::mutate(time = format(lubridate::with_tz(time, cfg$tz_local), "%d %b %H:%M:%S EST")) |>
  dplyr::select(time, selection, day, confidence, freq_low, freq_high) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**The time-zone trap.** `time` is stored and displayed in UTC, but local
time at the recorder is 5 hours behind. Taking the hour of day straight
from `time` shifts the whole diel cycle by 5 hours. Every hour in this
workflow is computed on `r cfg$tz_local` (EST; the IANA sign is inverted).
The log itself records every time with a fixed `-05:00` offset, even though
clocks were on EDT in late March. Sunset at the recorder was about 18:05
EST.

```{r}
#| label: tz-trap
#| fig-height: 3.5
by_hour <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(clock = "Hour taken from time (UTC): wrong",
                 hour = lubridate::hour(calls$time)),
  tibble::tibble(clock = "Hour on EST: used here",
                 hour = lubridate::hour(lubridate::with_tz(calls$time, cfg$tz_local)))
)
ggplot(by_hour, aes(hour)) +
  geom_bar(fill = pal[3]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 18.08, colour = grey[7], linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~clock) +
  labs(x = "Hour of day (dashed: sunset, 18:05 EST)", y = "Calls in the week")
```

## Calling over the week

```{r}
#| label: week
#| fig-height: 3.5
caveat <- lubridate::ymd_hm(c("2009-03-29 14:30", "2009-03-29 16:30"), tz = cfg$tz_local)
ggplot(bins, aes(bin, y)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = caveat[1], xmax = caveat[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = pal[2], alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_step(colour = grey[8]) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%d %b", date_breaks = "1 day", timezone = cfg$tz_local) +
  labs(x = "EST", y = paste("Calls per", cfg$bin_width, "min"),
       title = "Up-calls per bin; shaded: 29 March 14:30-16:30")
```

**Why 29 March 14:30–16:30 is kept.** The 2013 workshop's description of
this deployment warns that its analyst could not log reliably during
dense calling in that period. That warning was about those older logs.
The log used here is a later re-annotation of the same channel, and it
has heavy calling in that period. Recording was continuous, so the period
is not a gap in effort, and nothing in the NCEI metadata excludes it. It
is analysed like any other period. Excluding it would be a sensitivity
analysis, which this report does not run.

**Day 7 is complete.** The NCEI record gives the window as 28 March 00:00
to 4 April 00:00 EST, and the archive holds 672 contiguous 15-minute audio
files over that window. The last call, at 22:26 on 3 April, starts a quiet
spell; it is not where effort ended.

## Configuration in force

Every decision above, and in the models below, comes from `config.yml`.
These are the values that produced this report:

```{r}
#| label: config
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines("config.yml"), sep = "\n")
```

# Models

All four models are fitted to the same `r nrow(bins)` bins, with the count
per bin as the response and no offset (effort is the same in every bin).

1. **Poisson GLM.** A natural spline in time
   (`r cfg$models$glm_df` df) for the trend over the week, plus one
   sine/cosine pair for the diel cycle.
2. **Negative binomial GLM.** The same linear predictor, so the difference
   from the Poisson GLM is overdispersion alone.
3. **GAM LGCP.** This is a *GAM approximation to a log-Gaussian Cox
   process*, not an LGCP fitted in continuous time. The counts are Poisson
   given a latent Gaussian field on the log scale. The field has three
   parts: a Gaussian-process smooth of time (`k = `r cfg$models$k_time``),
   a cyclic smooth of hour of day (`k = `r cfg$models$k_hour``), and an
   independent normal "nugget" for each bin. With the nugget, each count
   is Poisson-lognormal. The fit uses `mgcv::bam` with fast REML.
4. **GAM LGCP + self-exciting.** The GAM LGCP with the same smooths,
   bases and `k`, plus a distributed-lag kernel. The log rate in each bin
   depends on `log1p` of the counts in the previous
   `r cfg$models$max_lag` bins
   (`r cfg$models$max_lag * cfg$bin_width / 60` hours). The kernel's
   shape is a smooth over lag, unconstrained in sign, so the data can show
   self-damping as well as self-excitation. This is a *log-linear
   self-exciting term, not a Hawkes process proper*: past calls multiply
   the rate rather than adding to it. Bins before the window are taken as
   zero counts.

The comparison asks whether recent calling predicts more calling *beyond*
a latent field of fixed flexibility.

# Comparison

```{r}
#| label: metrics
cmp$metrics |>
  dplyr::transmute(Model = label, `df / edf` = round(df, 1),
                   AIC = round(aic, 1), `ΔAIC` = round(d_aic, 1),
                   `CV log-lik` = round(cv_loglik, 1), `ΔCV` = round(d_cv, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

The table gives two criteria side by side and picks no winner. Lower
AIC is better, and higher CV log-likelihood is better; both Δ columns show
the distance from the best model.

- **AIC** for the GAMs is mgcv's conditional AIC, which counts the
  effective degrees of freedom of the smooths and the nugget.
- **CV** is leave-one-day-out: each model is refitted on six days and
  scored on the seventh. The GAMs have no estimate of the field on the
  held-out day, so they predict it from the field's distribution: the
  hour-of-day cycle plus a lognormal spread from the time smooth and the
  nugget.
- **The self-exciting model's CV score is one-step-ahead (conditional).**
  Its kernel is re-estimated in each fold. On the held-out day, each bin is
  predicted using that day's *observed* earlier counts. That uses
  information the other models do not, so its CV score answers a different
  question: how well can the next half hour be predicted, given the last
  six hours?

```{r}
#| label: cv-days
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(cmp$cv, aes(day, loglik, colour = lab(model))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = "Held-out day", y = "Predictive log-likelihood", colour = NULL,
       title = "Leave-one-day-out score per fold")
```

# Diagnostics

## Residuals

The residuals are randomised quantile residuals. If a model is right they
are standard normal and independent. The GAM residuals integrate over the
nugget, as the CV does. Otherwise each bin's own nugget would fit its
count almost exactly.

```{r}
#| label: resid-qq
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(cmp$resid, aes(sample = resid)) +
  geom_qq(colour = pal[1], size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(colour = grey[6]) +
  facet_wrap(~lab(model), nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Normal quantile", y = "Residual")
```

```{r}
#| label: resid-acf
#| fig-height: 4
bound <- 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(bins))
ggplot(cmp$resid_acf, aes(lag * cfg$bin_width / 60, acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-bound, bound), colour = grey[6], linetype = 2) +
  geom_col(fill = pal[1]) +
  facet_wrap(~lab(model), nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Lag (hours)", y = "Residual autocorrelation",
       title = "Serial dependence left over (dashed: ±1.96/√n)")
```

## Rootograms

Hanging rootograms compare the observed and expected number of bins with
each count. Bars hang from the expected curve, so a bar that ends above
zero means the model expects too many bins with that count, and one that
ends below zero means it expects too few. The square-root scale keeps
rare large counts visible.

```{r}
#| label: rootogram
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(cmp$rootogram, aes(count)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = count - 0.5, xmax = count + 0.5,
                ymax = sqrt(expected), ymin = sqrt(expected) - sqrt(observed)),
            fill = grey[4]) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sqrt(expected)), colour = pal[2]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = grey[8]) +
  facet_wrap(~lab(model), ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = paste("Calls per", cfg$bin_width, "min"), y = "√ number of bins")
```

## Basis size (`k.check`)

```{r}
#| label: kcheck
cmp$kcheck |>
  dplyr::transmute(Model = lab(model), Term = term, `k'` = `k'`, edf = round(edf, 1),
                   `k-index` = round(`k-index`, 2), `p-value` = signif(`p-value`, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

A k-index well below 1 with a small p-value usually means a basis is too
small. Here, for the time smooth, it does not. While building this
workflow, doubling `k_time` from 40 to 80 raised the smooth's edf but left
the k-index near 0.65, and AIC changed by about 1. The k-index measures
dependence between residuals of neighbouring bins, and what remains is
short-range clustering that the field's basis size cannot absorb. That is
the clustering the self-exciting term tests for. The nugget is left out:
a k-index means nothing for a random effect. The kernel has no k-index
because it is a sum over lags rather than a smooth of one covariate.

## Time smooths

```{r}
#| label: smooths
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(cmp$smooth, aes(bin, fit, colour = lab(model), fill = lab(model))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = fit - 1.96 * se, ymax = fit + 1.96 * se),
              alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols, aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%d %b", date_breaks = "1 day", timezone = cfg$tz_local) +
  labs(x = "EST", y = "s(t), log scale", colour = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Latent time smooth with and without the self-exciting term")
```

In the GAM LGCP the time smooth follows calling bout by bout
(edf `r round(cmp$kcheck$edf[cmp$kcheck$model == "lgcp" & cmp$kcheck$term == "s(t)"], 1)`).
Once the self-exciting term is added, much of that short-range structure
moves into the kernel, and the time smooth relaxes to a slow trend
(edf `r round(cmp$kcheck$edf[cmp$kcheck$model == "lgcp_se" & cmp$kcheck$term == "s(t)"], 1)`).
The two terms trade off against each other, and the data alone cannot fully
separate a smooth latent field from self-excitation.

## The self-exciting kernel

```{r}
#| label: kernel
#| fig-height: 3.5
kernel <- cmp$kernel |>
  dplyr::mutate(lo = fit - 1.96 * se, hi = fit + 1.96 * se,
                shape = dplyr::case_when(lo > 0 ~ "Excitatory",
                                         hi < 0 ~ "Damping",
                                         .default = "Flat (band covers 0)"))
ggplot(kernel, aes(hours, fit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = grey[6]) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = grey[3]) +
  geom_line(colour = grey[7]) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = shape), size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Excitatory = pal[2], Damping = pal[3],
                                 `Flat (band covers 0)` = grey[6])) +
  labs(x = "Lag (hours)", y = "Effect of log1p(count) on log rate",
       colour = NULL, title = "Fitted kernel with 95% band")
```

```{r}
#| label: kernel-tail
tail_flat <- all(kernel$shape[kernel$hours > max(kernel$hours) / 2] == "Flat (band covers 0)")
```

The kernel is the change in the log rate per unit of `log1p` count at
each lag. For example, 10 calls in the bin 30 minutes earlier multiply
the current rate by `r round(exp(log1p(10) * kernel$fit[1]), 1)`, with
everything else held fixed.
`r if (tail_flat) paste0("Over the second half of the ", max(kernel$hours), "-hour window every lag is flat, so the kernel has decayed well before the maximum lag and ", max(kernel$hours), " hours is long enough.") else paste0("Some lags in the second half of the ", max(kernel$hours), "-hour window are not flat, so the kernel may not have decayed by the maximum lag; consider a longer max_lag.")`
